TP63 is a p53-family transcription factor that acts canonically as a sequence-specific activator, binding response elements in the regulatory regions (promoter/enhancer) of its target genes and recruiting co-activators (p300/CBP, mediator) to drive RNA polymerase II initiation. Because ANKRD27 is listed as a TP63-regulated target, the inferred regulatory link is positive: TP63 occupancy supplies activating input to the ANKRD27 locus. When TP63 is lost or reduced, that activating input is removed — the response elements are no longer occupied, co-activator recruitment falls, and the basal transcriptional machinery at the ANKRD27 promoter runs at a lower rate. The causal order is therefore: TP63 protein loss (perturbation) → loss of TF occupancy at ANKRD27 regulatory elements → reduced co-activator/Pol II engagement → decreased ANKRD27 mRNA. So relative to the matched unperturbed control, ANKRD27 expression is expected to go down. (Caveat: if the specific mechanism were direct repression rather than activation, the sign would invert; the activator interpretation is the default for this TF–target relationship.)

TP63 encodes p63, a p53-family transcription factor that acts canonically as a sequence-specific activator: it binds response elements in the promoters/enhancers of its target genes and recruits coactivators (e.g., p300/CBP) to drive RNA polymerase II initiation. Here TIMM50 — the mitochondrial inner-membrane translocase subunit — is a direct transcriptional target in the TP63 regulatory network, so the causal order is TP63 binding → increased TIMM50 transcription → higher TIMM50 mRNA/protein. Reducing or losing TP63 removes that activating input, so the promoter is no longer occupied and transcription of TIMM50 falls; the readout relative to the matched unperturbed control therefore moves downward. The key mediator of the change is loss of p63 occupancy (and consequent loss of coactivator recruitment) at the TIMM50 locus rather than any post-transcriptional step, meaning the drop should appear at the nascent-transcript/mRNA level first.

Causal chain: ESR1 (ERα) is the activating input at the MMP17 enhancer cluster — the MMP17-1 ERBS carries a full ERE and sits at the top of a hierarchical pair of ER-bound sites, recruiting ERα and establishing the active H3K27ac/accessible chromatin state, with MMP17-2 then binding ERα and contributing to promoter activity. ERα occupancy at those sites is what transmits the estrogen signal to the MMP17 promoter, and MMP17 is strongly induced downstream of that axis (e.g. ~14-fold E2 induction in Ishikawa cells, versus no induction in T-47D where those ERBS lack ER binding and H3K27ac). So removing or reducing ESR1 — or deleting the target regulatory site itself — strips the enhancer of its activator: ER occupancy at the ERE is lost first, enhancer activity and chromatin accessibility collapse, the promoter's activation signal disappears, and MMP17 transcription falls. Order: ESR1 loss → loss of ER at the MMP17 ERBS cluster → loss of enhancer/promoter activation → decreased MMP17 mRNA. (Cell-type context matters: this direction holds in ER-dependent, ERBS-active contexts.)

GATA1 is a direct transcriptional activator of Slc4a1 (erythroid band 3/AE1): it occupies the GATA motifs in the Slc4a1 promoter and erythroid enhancer and recruits coactivators such as CBP/p300 and the Mediator complex to drive transcription. The R216Q substitution sits in the N-terminal zinc finger, the domain that stabilizes GATA1 on palindromic GATA sites (and mediates FOG1/ZFPM1 interaction), so the mutant protein binds its cognate sites in the Slc4a1 regulatory region less stably. Order of events: R216Q variant → weakened GATA1 DNA occupancy at Slc4a1 cis-elements → loss of coactivator recruitment and reduced promoter/enhancer activity → lower Slc4a1 mRNA. Hence, relative to the matched unperturbed control, Slc4a1 expression decreases.

FOXC1e is the upstream input for this pair — the regulatory element/regulator through which ESR1 acts on the FOXC1 locus — so it sits above FOXC1 in the causal chain. Removing or reducing it severs that input: less activator is present at the FOXC1 promoter/enhancer, co-activator recruitment and transcription-initiation complex assembly drop, and the rate of FOXC1 transcription falls, so mature FOXC1 mRNA accumulates to a lower steady-state level than in the matched unperturbed control. Order of events: loss of FOXC1e activity → reduced ESR1-dependent activation of the FOXC1 locus → decreased FOXC1 transcription → lower FOXC1 expression. No feedback loop that would restore or overshoot FOXC1 is specified, so the direction is downward.

SIAH2 is the perturbed entity itself, so the loss-of-function perturbation (CRISPRi/knockdown/knockout) acts directly on the SIAH2 locus: transcription of SIAH2 mRNA is reduced and, because SIAH2 is an E3 ubiquitin–ligase whose own abundance is short-lived, protein follows quickly. The upstream regulator in this context, ESR1, sits earlier in the chain and drives SIAH2 transcription; any indirect compensation would have to run in the reverse order — loss of SIAH2 relieves its destabilization of ESR1, raising ESR1 and secondarily SIAH2 transcription — but that is a delayed, downstream feedback loop and cannot outrun the primary loss of SIAH2 transcript/protein within the assay window. Net effect relative to the matched unperturbed control: SIAH2 expression decreases.

BHLHE40 (DEC1/Stra13) is a bHLH-Orange protein that works as a transcriptional repressor rather than an activator, and in hepatocytes it restrains the PPARα arm of the lipid-handling program — it lowers Ppara itself and competes for binding at PPAR response elements. Angptl4/FIAF is one of the canonical PPRE-driven PPARα targets, so with BHLHE40 knocked down that brake comes off: PPARA level and activity rise first, occupancy at the Angptl4 promoter goes up second, and Angptl4 transcription follows. Losing a repressor of the upstream regulator therefore shifts the target upward relative to the matched control.

ZNF143 (Staf/SBF) is a zinc-finger transcription factor that binds its cognate SBS/SPH motif in promoters and acts as a transcriptional activator, recruiting co-activators and contributing to promoter–enhancer looping. Because ANKRD13B is a positively regulated ZNF143 target, reducing ZNF143 removes that activating input at the ANKRD13B regulatory element: the primary event is loss of ZNF143 occupancy at the gene's promoter/regulatory region, which is followed by reduced co-activator recruitment, decreased RNA Pol II initiation/pausing release, and consequently lower ANKRD13B mRNA. The direction is therefore downward — loss of an activator lowers, not raises, its target. (This assumes the documented regulation is direct and activating, as stated; were the effect indirect — e.g., ZNF143 repressing a repressor — the sign could invert, but the stated mechanism gives a decrease.)

ZNF143 is a C2H2 zinc-finger transcription factor that acts as a promoter-bound activator: it recognizes its cognate SBS motif in the CCDC157 promoter, recruits coactivators and helps assemble/stabilize the RNA polymerase II preinitiation complex. The causal order is therefore: loss or reduction of ZNF143 → decreased ZNF143 occupancy at the CCDC157 promoter → reduced coactivator recruitment and Pol II loading → lower CCDC157 transcription initiation → decreased CCDC157 mRNA. Because the regulator being removed is the activating input rather than a repressive one, the matched unperturbed control (ZNF143 intact) sits at the higher expression level, so CCDC157 is expected to go down after the perturbation.

ZNF143 is a sequence-specific activator that occupies the SBS/Staf motif in the promoters of its target genes and recruits coactivators to support RNA polymerase II initiation. A loss-or-reduction perturbation removes that activating input at the CPSF4 promoter, so the key mediator — promoter-bound ZNF143-dependent recruitment of Pol II and its coactivators — can no longer be assembled at normal levels. The order is therefore: ZNF143 depletion → reduced ZNF143 occupancy at the CPSF4 promoter → diminished transcriptional initiation → lower CPSF4 mRNA and protein output, i.e. expression moves down relative to the matched unperturbed control.

Explanation: ZNF143 is a zinc-finger transcription factor that acts as a promoter-bound activator, recognizing the ZNF143/SPH motif (SBS) and recruiting coactivators and RNA polymerase II to drive transcription. With ZNF143 lost or reduced, occupancy at the EMC1 regulatory region drops, so the ordered chain is: ZNF143 protein depletion → loss of promoter/enhancer binding at its cognate SBS motif → reduced Pol II recruitment and transcription initiation → lower EMC1 mRNA (and subsequently less EMC1 protein) relative to the matched unperturbed control in the same cell context. Note this assumes the annotated regulatory link is activating (the mechanism field given is empty); if ZNF143 were instead acting as a repressor at this locus, the direction would invert.

ZNF143 (the human Staf homolog) is a sequence-specific C2H2 zinc-finger **transcriptional activator** that occupies high-affinity SBS1/SBS2 motifs in the promoters of ~3,000 mostly housekeeping genes. GAMT, the guanidinoacetate N-methyltransferase gene that carries out the final step of creatine biosynthesis, is a ubiquitous metabolic/housekeeping promoter of exactly this class, so the regulatory mechanism is direct promoter activation rather than repression. The causal order is: ZNF143 loss-of-function → loss of ZNF143 occupancy at the GAMT promoter → failure to nucleate the pre-initiation complex and its coactivators (ZNF143 acts early, recruiting POU2F1/HCF-1 and stabilizing the Pol II machinery at G1; its degradation acutely reduces transcription initiation) → reduced RNA Pol II initiation at the GAMT TSS → lower GAMT mRNA. The key mediator is therefore ZNF143's activator function at the GAMT promoter itself, with the drop in nascent transcription preceding any secondary change in the creatine-pathway metabolite flux. Note the one caveat: ZNF143 also directly represses a minority of genes by promoter occlusion/roadblocking, so if GAMT belonged to that repressed subset the sign would flip — but for a metabolic housekeeping gene bound at the TSS with the canonical SBS motif, the expected direction is down.

down

ZNF143 (SBF/STAF) is a sequence-specific C2H2 zinc-finger transcription factor whose canonical, genome-wide role is activation: it recognizes the Staf-binding site (SBS) present in thousands of promoters, recruits cofactors including CHD8 and the HCFC1–THAP11 module, and stimulates RNA polymerase II initiation. For a gene such as JMJD8 that is annotated as a ZNF143-regulated target, the promoter binding is therefore expected to be activating, so removing ZNF143 — by knockdown, degron-mediated degradation, or knockout — eliminates the activator at the JMJD8 promoter, reduces initiation (and, secondarily, promoter-proximal pausing release and elongation), and the mature JMJD8 transcript falls relative to the matched unperturbed control. Order of events: ZNF143 loss → loss of SBS occupancy and coactivator recruitment at the JMJD8 promoter → decreased Pol II initiation and nascent transcription → lower steady-state JMJD8 mRNA. One caveat worth flagging: ZNF143 is bifunctional and directly represses a minority of genes by occluding the TSS or blocking early elongation, so if this particular annotation were built on a repression mechanism the prediction would invert; on the default activator interpretation, and given that JMJD8 has no reported ZNF143-dependent repression, the expected direction is down.

ZNF143 binds the SPH/STAF-type motif in the LATS1 promoter and functions as a transcriptional activator, recruiting general transcription factors and coactivators that sustain LATS1 mRNA synthesis. When ZNF143 is reduced or lost, promoter occupancy drops first, which lowers the initiation rate of LATS1 transcription and, over time, the steady-state level of LATS1 mRNA and protein. The causal order is therefore: ZNF143 loss → reduced promoter binding/coactivator recruitment → decreased LATS1 transcription → lower LATS1 expression, with no competing compensatory activation expected at the timescale of a standard perturbation experiment.

ZNF143 (also known as SBF/STAF) is a promoter-bound, largely activating transcription factor: it binds a 29-bp motif near TSSs and recruits the general initiation machinery, so it stimulates RNA Polymerase II initiation at the majority of its direct targets — acute degron-mediated depletion of ZNF143 in human cells down-regulates hundreds of genes, while only a small minority (bound at genic rather than promoter positions, typically occluding YY1/SP1 sites or blocking early elongation) go up. For MTMR1, binding of ZNF143 at the promoter places it in the activating class: the primary, cell-autonomous step is loss of ZNF143 occupancy at the MTMR1 promoter, which lowers initiation complex recruitment and reduces nascent MTMR1 transcription, producing a drop in mature MTMR1 mRNA within roughly 30–120 minutes, ahead of any secondary changes in PI3P/membrane-trafficking pathway output. So the order is ZNF143 protein loss → loss of promoter occupancy/initiation → decreased MTMR1 transcription → decreased MTMR1 mRNA and protein. One caveat: if this particular context places ZNF143 in its repressive, genic-binding mode, the sign would invert — but the promoter-proximal, activator class is the expected default for MTMR1.

ZNF143 binds the PRIM1 promoter directly through its Staf/ZNF143 recognition motif and acts there as a transcriptional activator, recruiting general initiation machinery (and cofactors such as HCF-1/THAP11 at cell-cycle and DNA-replication genes) to stimulate RNA Pol II initiation. PRIM1, the catalytic subunit of DNA primase, is one of the replication/cell-cycle genes in this ZNF143-driven program. So in the order of events: loss or reduction of ZNF143 → its promoter occupancy at PRIM1 is lost → initiation frequency and nascent transcription at the PRIM1 promoter fall → mature PRIM1 mRNA declines, relative to the matched unperturbed control in the same cellular context. (Note: ZNF143 also represses a smaller subset of direct targets, which go up upon depletion — but PRIM1 is a promoter-bound activated target, so the expected direction is down.)

ZNF143 is a sequence-specific activator: it binds SBS1/SBS2 motifs in target promoters and recruits the general initiation machinery (TFIIA/SAGA-associated cofactors, via its N-terminal activation domain) to stimulate RNA Pol II transcription initiation. For the majority of its direct targets, acute loss of ZNF143 — by degron-mediated degradation or knockdown — abolishes promoter occupancy and reduces initiation, producing a drop in nascent transcription within minutes to hours. RDH11 is a promoter-proximal, widely expressed gene recovered as a ZNF143-bound target in GTRD/ReMap ChIP evidence, so the causal chain runs ZNF143 depletion → loss of its occupancy at the RDH11 promoter → reduced Pol II initiation and promoter-proximal pausing release → falling RDH11 nascent transcript → falling mature RDH11 mRNA and retinol-dehydrogenase protein. The caveat worth flagging is directionality: ZNF143 also cis-represses a minority of genes bound near their transcription start site, and those go *up* on depletion — but that is the exception, and for the canonical activator-mode relationship with RDH11 the expectation is downregulation.

ZNF143 acts as a sequence-specific activator at the Staf-binding site (SBS) promoter motif, where it recruits the basal machinery (TFIID/TAF1-associated, RNA Pol II initiation) rather than repressing it. Because SAMD13 sits downstream of ZNF143 in this activation relationship, reducing ZNF143 lowers promoter occupancy and co-activator recruitment at the SAMD13 promoter, which decreases the rate of transcriptional initiation and therefore the steady-state SAMD13 mRNA level — the direction of the change is transmitted TF → promoter binding → transcription, so the target follows the direction of the regulator (activator loss gives target loss). One caveat worth stating: this assumes the documented activator mode is what operates at this locus; if ZNF143 were instead acting as a tethered repressor at SAMD13 (e.g., via a co-repressor complex), the sign would invert, so the causal chain here gives down, not up.

ZNF143 is a sequence-specific activator (a CCAAT-box/SPH-type zinc-finger factor that binds promoters and enhancers and promotes transcription). In the described regulatory edge, ZNF143 acts upstream as the direct positive regulator of SLC9A6 — the causal order is ZNF143 binding to the SLC9A6 regulatory region → recruitment of coactivators and assembly of the transcription machinery → productive SLC9A6 transcription. Because the mechanism is activation rather than repression, loss or reduction of ZNF143 removes that activating input, so SLC9A6 mRNA output falls relative to the matched unperturbed control (with the possibility of secondary, indirect effects on the gene's regulatory network arriving later, after the initial loss of direct promoter occupancy).

ZNF143 is a sequence-specific activating transcription factor: it binds promoter-proximal SPH/motif elements and recruits coactivators and the RNA Pol II machinery to drive transcription. TFAM is a nuclear-encoded gene, so its expression depends on this promoter-bound activator rather than on mitochondrial transcription. When ZNF143 is lost or reduced, the TFAM promoter loses its activator occupancy — coactivator and Pol II recruitment at that promoter fall, the initiation rate drops, and TFAM mRNA (and consequently protein) declines relative to the matched unperturbed control. Order: ZNF143 depletion → loss of ZNF143 binding at the TFAM promoter → reduced coactivator/Pol II recruitment → decreased TFAM transcription → lower TFAM expression. Since the mechanism is activator loss, there is no compensatory derepression, so the direction is down.

ZNF143 acts as a promoter-bound transcriptional activator: it recognizes its cognate SBS motif in the TOMM70 promoter and recruits/assembles the general transcription machinery to drive RNA polymerase II initiation. When ZNF143 is lost or reduced, that activating input at the TOMM70 promoter is removed, so the rate of TOMM70 transcription falls first, the mature TOMM70 mRNA pool shrinks next, and the TOMM70 protein level follows. In order: ZNF143 depletion → loss of promoter occupancy/activation → reduced TOMM70 transcription → lower TOMM70 mRNA (and subsequently protein). The direction is therefore down, not up; a rise would only be expected if ZNF143 were acting as a repressor, which is not its canonical role here.

ZNF143 acts as a transcriptional activator at the ZBTB10 promoter, so reducing ZNF143 protein lowers its occupancy at the ZBTB10 regulatory region and the gene's transcription rate falls. The causal order is: ZNF143 loss → reduced promoter binding/activation → less ZBTB10 mRNA (and subsequently less ZBTB10 protein). The effect is direct and primary (no intermediate mediator required), though because it operates on transcription, the drop in mature ZBTB10 transcript will lag the perturbation somewhat and will be graded according to how complete the knockdown is.

ZNF143 is a transcriptional activator — it binds its cognate GTGGC/CCACC-type motif at promoters and enhancers and recruits the machinery that drives transcription. Here it is the upstream regulator and ZNF382 the target, so ZNF382 expression is sustained by ZNF143 occupancy at its regulatory elements. When ZNF143 is lost or reduced, that activating input disappears: ZNF143 loss → reduced ZNF143 occupancy at the ZNF382 promoter/enhancer → less transcriptional activation → lower ZNF382 mRNA relative to the matched unperturbed control. The key mediator is ZNF143's direct binding at the ZNF382 locus (not a downstream relay), and the effect is directional and proximal — the target decays within the timescale of the transcription/degradation kinetics, so the decrease is expected rather than a secondary compensation that could later push it back up.

NANOG sits in a positive autoregulatory loop: the protein binds its own promoter/enhancer (in complex with OCT4 and SOX2) and sustains its own transcription, so removing NANOG protein strips away a direct activator input at the Nanog locus — reduced promoter occupancy, less RNA Pol II recruitment, and a rapid fall in Nanog transcript. The effect then compounds: NANOG also maintains the broader pluripotency network (Pou5f1, Sox2), loss of which further erodes Nanog transcription, so the initial direct drop feeds back into a deeper decline and eventual differentiation-associated silencing. Order is direct-promoter first, network-mediated reinforcement second — never up, since Nanog has no NANOG-independent repression relief that would outweigh the lost activation.

up

miR-210 is a hypoxia-inducible microRNA whose transcription is driven by HIF1A, and it acts downstream as a direct post-transcriptional repressor of E2F3 — its seed sequence pairs with the E2F3 3′UTR, recruiting the RISC to degrade or translationally silence the transcript. The functional order is therefore HIF1A → miR-210 ⊣ E2F3: HIF1A is the upstream inducer of the miRNA, and the miRNA is the proximate negative regulator of the target. When miR-210 is lost or knocked down, that repressive arm is removed while HIF1A-driven transcription is untouched, so E2F3 mRNA and protein are de-repressed and rise above the matched control level. The effect is graded by the extent of miR-210 depletion and is most pronounced in a hypoxic/HIF1A-active background, where miR-210 is abundant and its repression of E2F3 is normally strongest.

up

UHRF1 is the terminal effector of the PPARA repression module, not an activator of it. In this axis PPARA is autoinduced and drives E2f8, and E2F8 in turn drives Uhrf1; UHRF1 is then recruited to promoters that carry the H3K9me3 mark, where it loads DNMT1 and HDAC1 and installs promoter DNA methylation that silences them. Cdh3 belongs to precisely that H3K9me3-marked, UHRF1-dependent repressed gene set (alongside Cdh1, Smpd3, Mir99ahg and Mirlet7c-1), and UHRF1 knockdown is documented to reverse repression of these cadherin genes. Losing UHRF1 therefore removes the methylation-based silencing at the Cdh3 promoter, so Cdh3 is de-repressed and rises. Order of events on the perturbation: UHRF1 loss → loss of DNMT1/HDAC1 recruitment to the H3K9me3-marked Cdh3 promoter → promoter demethylation/local chromatin de-repression → increased Cdh3 transcription, with PPARA levels themselves unchanged.

down

MYC binds E-box elements (the CACATG/CACGTG consensus) as an obligate heterodimer with MAX and acts predominantly as a transcriptional activator at these sites, recruiting coactivators such as TRRAP, GCN5/p300 and the P-TEFb kinase to drive RNA Pol II pause release and productive elongation at its target promoters. The perturbed element — the MYC E-box at chr10_BS212 (CACATG) — is the cis-regulatory docking site through which MYC is recruited to the PRKCQ-AS1 locus, so removing or disrupting that motif abolishes MYC occupancy there. With the activator no longer tethered, the local activating histone marks and Pol II elongation stimulus are lost, and PRKCQ-AS1 transcription falls. Order of events: E-box motif lost → MYC–MAX cannot bind the locus → loss of coactivator recruitment and Pol II pause release → decreased PRKCQ-AS1 transcription. Hence expression is expected to go **down** relative to the matched unperturbed control.

down

FOXK1 is a tumor-selective partner of the lineage master TF TP63 in squamous carcinoma, where it binds (together with p63) at the anchors of p63-dependent 3D chromatin loops and is required to maintain them. NABP2 sits in the "Secondary" mode of this architecture: its promoter contacts a p63-bound enhancer indirectly, through a FOXK1-associated intermediate anchor, and FOXK1 occupancy at those anchors is what holds the loop together. When FOXK1 is lost or reduced, the p63-dependent secondary loop at NABP2 weakens (27.6% of p63-dependent loops carry FOXK1 at an anchor, and p63-dependent loops are preferentially lost upon FOXK1 KO), the enhancer–promoter contact is no longer sustained, and transcription of the linked target falls; p63 protein itself is largely unaffected (~85% remaining), so the effect is carried by FOXK1-dependent loop maintenance rather than by loss of p63. Order of events: FOXK1 loss → weakened p63-dependent secondary loop at NABP2 → reduced NABP2 mRNA (confirmed by RT-qPCR alongside HNRNPA1, HNRNPL, RPS16 and other Secondary-mode targets). Hence NABP2 expression goes down relative to the matched unperturbed control.

Perturbing the E2 regulatory site removes the STAT3 docking element from the Klf4 locus, so the causal chain runs: STAT3 (activated by upstream LIF/IL-6-family cytokine signaling) can no longer bind E2 → loss of STAT3-driven transcriptional activation at that cis-element → reduced Klf4 promoter/enhancer activity → less Klf4 mRNA, and secondarily less Klf4 protein. The key mediator is STAT3 acting as a direct activator through E2, with the site itself as the order-limiting step: the perturbation precedes and prevents STAT3 occupancy, which precedes the drop in transcription. Relative to the matched unperturbed control, Klf4 expression therefore goes down.

CTCF is not a classical sequence-specific activator here; it works as an architectural anchor. At CUL3 regulatory site A, CTCF binds its cognate core motif and recruits cohesin (RAD21/SMC1/3), which stabilizes a chromatin loop that holds the element in physical contact with the CUL3 promoter and its enhancers. Perturbing site A — by CRISPRi/CRISPRa tiling, motif mutation, or dCas9-KRAB occlusion — abolishes CTCF occupancy, so cohesin unloads, the loop and enhancer–promoter contact are lost, and the promoter loses its activation input. Order of events: site A perturbation → loss of CTCF binding → cohesin eviction and loop dissolution → reduced enhancer–promoter contact and RNA Pol II at the CUL3 promoter → lower CUL3 mRNA. Note the caveat that if site A were instead acting as an insulator between CUL3 and a distal enhancer, loss of binding would de-repress and give the opposite result; the direction above assumes the anchoring/loop-bridging mode, which is the mechanism implied by the stated CTCF–CUL3 relationship.

KMT2D (MLL4) is the principal H3K4 mono-/dimethyltransferase acting at enhancers, where it deposits H3K4me1/me2 and helps keep chromatin accessible for lineage transcription factors. ZFPM1 (FOG1) is a direct GATA1 target whose erythroid/megakaryocytic expression depends on GATA1-bound enhancer elements that carry those active H3K4 marks. When KMT2D is lost, H3K4 methylation at these GATA1-occupied enhancers collapses, GATA1 recruitment and enhancer-promoter looping are weakened, and transcription of the target locus falls — so ZFPM1 goes down, downstream of reduced GATA1-driven enhancer activity (KMT2D → H3K4me1/2 at GATA1 enhancers → GATA1 occupancy/transactivation → ZFPM1 transcription).

Down.

Because ETV4 (PEA3), the ETS-family factor in question, is a sequence-specific transcriptional activator that binds ETS motifs in the NOTCH4 regulatory region and drives its transcription; when ETV4 is lost or reduced, those activating complexes are no longer recruited to the NOTCH4 promoter/enhancer, so NOTCH4 mRNA output falls. The order is: ETV4 depletion → loss of ETV4 occupancy at NOTCH4 regulatory elements → reduced RNA polymerase II loading and transcription → lower NOTCH4 expression relative to the matched unperturbed control. (Caveat: this assumes ETV4 acts as a positive regulator of NOTCH4 in that context; if the mechanism were instead ETV4-mediated repression, the direction would invert.)
